stories.headline: Drug war is everyone’s fight: DGP Prabhat
stories.title: Drug war is everyone’s fight: DGP Prabhat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 12: Director General of Police (DGP) Nalin Prabhat on Monday called for a united societal response to the growing challenge of drug abuse, asserting that protecting children and young people from narcotics was a collective responsibility that extended far beyond the police force. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a function at Police Public School here, the DGP said the campaign against drugs was gaining momentum across Jammu and Kashmir under the leadership of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha. He said the future of the country depended on safeguarding its younger generation from substance abuse. “These small children are the future of our country,” Prabhat said, underlining the need for society to come together to protect young people from the menace. Referring to recent enforcement action against drug trafficking in Srinagar, the J&K Police chief said several arrests had been made as part of the crackdown. He emphasised that tackling the problem required a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, with active participation from citizens. “It is our duty that we participate in this fight and say no to drugs,” he said, urging people to join the campaign against narcotics. The DGP's appeal comes as Jammu & Kashmir Police intensifies efforts to raise awareness about drug abuse alongside enforcement action against traffickers. The emphasis on community participation places families, educational institutions and local communities at the centre of efforts to prevent substance abuse and protect vulnerable youth. As part of the awareness drive, the DGP flagged off a motorcycle rally from Police Public School, Bemina, Srinagar, towards Ekta Nagar in Gujarat for the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade scheduled for October 31. The contingent comprises 10 bikers from Jammu and Kashmir Police and five from Ladakh Police. Awareness programmes on the harmful effects of drug abuse are planned along the route, with a focus on sensitising young people and promoting the message of a drug-free society. The initiative combines public outreach with the broader campaign against narcotics, seeking to carry the message beyond police establishments and into communities. The DGP’s message was clear-- enforcement against traffickers must go hand in hand with public awareness, prevention and collective responsibility if Jammu and Kashmir is to protect its next generation from the consequences of drug abuse.

stories.title: 6.1 earthquake jolts southern Panama after Friday's destructive tremors
stories.summary: Panama City, Oct 13: A preliminary magnitude 6.1 earthquake hit southern Panama Monday evening, according to the US Geological Survey, but there were no immediate reports of casualties or property damage. The quake struck around 6:20 p.m. at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles) about 18 kilometers (11 miles) west of Río Grande in the country's south. The quake comes after two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks roiled southern Panama on Friday afternoon. They collapsed buildings near the epicenter and prompted evacuations across the country.

stories.headline: Winning, differently: On the by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry
stories.title: Winning, differently: On the by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry
stories.summary: Ruling parties sweep by-elections, but defections mar Tamil Nadu results
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'election results' in title weight 64
article_sentences: The by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, declared on Friday, held few surprises.
Barely five months after the April Assembly elections, the ruling party in each State/UT won all five bypolls.
What varied was the scale of victory.
In West Bengal, the BJP retained Nandigram and wrested Rejinagar, with strong vote shares of 76% and 63%.
In Puducherry, the ruling.
All India N.R. Congress also registered an emphatic win — 61% of the votes — in Thattanchavady.
Nandigram and Thattanchavady were vacated by the Chief Ministers, which partly explains the strong wins.
But the contests in Tamil Nadu were closer.
Dharapuram and Madurantakam fell vacant after their AIADMK MLAs resigned and defected to the ruling TVK, which renominated them.
Both won their seats back with 37% and 40% of the vote, respectively, leading the DMK rival candidates by about eight percentage points.
By-elections tend to favour the party in power, as voters prefer representatives with access to government.
But the variance between West Bengal and Tamil Nadu reflects the nature of contest in two similarly sized States but with vastly different political cultures.

stories.headline: Karnataka High Court Directs Police To Secure LOC Against Husband In Dowry Case
stories.title: Karnataka High Court Directs Police To Secure LOC Against Husband In Dowry Case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Karnataka High Court on Monday [October 12] directed the police to take steps for the issuance of the Look Out Circular (LOC) against the husband of a woman who has accused him of cruelty and dowry harassment, while ordering hand delivery of the order.

The single judge bench of Justice Anant Ramananth Hegde passed the interim direction while hearing a criminal petition filed by the wife seeking a direction to the police to issue LOC against her husband- a working professional at France.
The direction is subject to Court's final order.

The wife has contended that her husband remains in India only for the reissuance of his supposedly lost passport, and that his departure afterwards would irretrievably damage her cause and further investigation in the FIR.
The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) had in October rejected her application under Section 175(3) r/w Section 94 of the BNSS for the same reliefs.

Yesterday, when the matter was taken up, Advocate Angad Kamath, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that not intimating the respondent husband about the issuance of the LOC would not infringe upon his rights under the Constitution of India, and that the LOC can be issued subject to the guidelines issued therein.

“…It is well settled that mere inability to pay the money without there being a criminal case cannot be a reason to take away the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India…”.

Kamath submitted that while dowry harassment is part of the allegations, the purported inability to pay money by the accused, as mentioned by the magistrate in the order, had nothing to do with the case or the issuance of the LOC sought for.
He pointed out that there are two named accused, the mother-in-law and the husband.
The husband is a resident of France, and once he goes back, he cannot be secured for investigation.
Though he is a passport holder of India, he has been a resident of France for 3 years, Kamath added.
He holds a visa of Tunisia and France, and all he requires is a boarding pass to leave the country forever, it was submitted further.

stories.headline: Say no to drugs, protect future: DGP Nalin Prabhat
stories.title: Say no to drugs, protect future: DGP Nalin Prabhat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 12: Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat on Monday called for a whole-of-society approach in the fight against drug abuse, even as he flagged off a National Motorcycle Rally carrying the message of a Nasha Mukt society. Speaking to mediapersons on the sidelines of the programme here at Police Public School, the DGP said the anti-drug campaign was being pursued across the country and had gained considerable momentum in Jammu and Kashmir under the leadership of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha. Referring to recent enforcement action in the summer capital Srinagar, he said that several people had been arrested as part of the ongoing crackdown. “These small children are the future of our country,” Prabhat told reporters, stressing that protecting the younger generation from substance abuse was a shared responsibility. He described the campaign as a collective fight that required more than law enforcement action alone. “This is a war being fought across society, with a whole-of-government approach. It is our duty that we participate in this fight and say no to drugs,” he said. The DGP said this after flagging off the motorcycle rally comprising 10 bikers of the Jammu and Kashmir Police and five from the Ladakh Police. The contingent is headed for Ekta Nagar in Gujarat and will form part of the nationwide contingents converging for the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas Parade on October 31, 2026, to mark the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. The theme of the rally is “Fight Against Drugs,” and the participants will conduct awareness programmes en route to sensitise people, particularly the youth. Prior to the flag-off, an awareness programme on the fight against drugs was held at the school, drawing enthusiastic participation from a large number of students. Senior officers present included Special DG Coordination S.J.M. Gillani, Additional DG Armed Nitish Kumar, IGP Headquarters Bhim Sen Tuti, IGP Kashmir Sujit Kumar and DIG Armed Range Kashmir Maqsood-ul-Zaman, the nodal officer for the J&K Police contingent. Nalin Prabhat expressed satisfaction over the initiatives being undertaken to realise the vision of the Prime Minister and the Lieutenant Governor towards building a drug-free society. He also appreciated the participation of the J&K Police in the national motorcycle rally, in which 45 contingents from states, Union Territories and Central Armed Police Forces are taking part.

stories.headline: Saudis probe how defence systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
stories.title: Saudis probe how defence systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 13: Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defences failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defence systems used by the Saudis. One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defence systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 1,000 kilometres (620 miles) to reach Riyadh. The incident, one of a string of Houthi attacks since last week on Saudi airports, has exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi Arabia's defence system and signalled a dangerous inflexion point in an expanding Middle East conflict that began more than seven months ago when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran. The Saudi-led coalition also said it had twice intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched Monday by Yemen's Houthi rebels toward Riyadh. At least three explosions could be heard Monday night in the city. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Civil Defence officials later said the danger had passed. Earlier on Monday, the Saudi state-run media reported that its military was responding to a new attack involving drones and cruise missiles, but provided no details. “The events of recent weeks are serious," Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the World Petroleum Energy Congress in Riyadh on Monday. “Our response must be equally serious.” The Saudi government-run Centre for International Communication, which oversees foreign media, did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the probe into defence failures. Saudi officials want more US help in countering Houthi attacks The Saudis want the US to become more directly involved in their fight against the Houthis. The US has provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for a Saudi-led offensive, but has held off on carrying out strikes against the Houthis. A US intervention could prompt the Houthis to try to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The flow of Middle East oil has already been complicated by Iranian efforts to choke off the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil flowed before the US-Iran war began. The rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government, has been trying to retake them. US President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday after the deadly airport strike that he was looking at the possibility of carrying out US attacks against the Houthis. But the conflict comes at a delicate time for Trump, just weeks before US midterm elections that will decide if his Republican Party keeps control of Congress. Persistent inflation and high gas prices fueled by the ongoing conflict with Iran have driven widespread American disapproval of that war. Expanding US military involvement in the region risks further stoking voters' resentment. Houthis say Saudis launch new attacks Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said Monday that airstrikes on a government complex and a house in the northern province of al-Jawf killed nine people, including five children and a woman, and wounded seven others, according to the Houthi-controlled SABA news agency. Houthi officials also said that Saudi Arabia carried out new strikes on the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, killing one person and wounding 12. The Riyadh airport remained closed on Monday, and workers in the capital's financial district were told to work from home. Yet, the Saudis on Monday continued with the second day of the World Petroleum Energy Congress. UAE diplomat suggests Gulf allies respond to Houthis jointly Separately, an Emirati diplomat on Monday called for “joint Gulf action” to defend Gulf countries against attacks by Iran and its allied groups. Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the rulers of the United Arab Emirates, said Iran and its allies wrongly assessed that Gulf Arabs were “the weakest link” in the US war against Iran, during which Tehran and its allies repeatedly attacked Arab countries on the other side of the Gulf. “It has become clear that we are all targeted, and that our security is indivisible,” he wrote on social media. Iran's Foreign Ministry on Monday expressed concern about fighting between the Saudis and Houthis and said Iran would be ready to settle disputes. “We are severely concerned about developments in the Arabian Peninsula,” spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at his weekly briefing. “We have many times announced readiness for applying our good offices in order to facilitate talks between the two sides.” Baghaei said Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al-Saud, spoke by phone on Sunday about the situation but did not offer details. Funeral held for Jordanian killed in airport attack Dozens of mourners attended the Monday funeral for a Jordanian killed in the missile strike on King Khalid International Airport. Mahmoud Al-Barqawi, 33, who worked in a Riyadh cafe and was the father of two children, was buried after a funeral procession began at a mosque in Amman. His father, Hasan al-Barqawi, said the family was struggling to cope. “No one can truly feel the pain of this tragedy,” he said. The strike also wounded four Jordanian citizens. Jordan's Royal Court chief Yousef Al-Issawi attended the funeral, offering condolences on behalf of the king and crown prince.

stories.headline: Russian diesel for America: The double standards in Trump’s energy policy needs an answer
stories.title: Russian diesel for America: The double standards in Trump’s energy policy needs an answer
stories.summary: New Delhi, October 12: Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel exposes the gap between Washington’s energy needs and its demands on others. India must defend its right to make independent choices based on national interest. US President Donald Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel into American markets has raised an important question about the consistency of Washington’s policy towards Moscow. For years, the United States has pressured India to reduce/stop its purchases of Russian oil, arguing that the revenue helps finance Russia’s war against Ukraine. Now, when rising fuel prices threaten American consumers and the Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections, Trump himself has turned to Russia for supplies. The visible difference is clear. When India buys Russian oil, the US raises objections. But when America needs Russian diesel, it finds a way to make the deal happen. This raises questions about fairness and whether every country has the right to take decisions based on its own needs without facing political pressure. America puts its own interests first. Trump has announced a deal under which Russia will supply diesel to the US and other markets in the coming months. To make this possible, his administration has temporarily relaxed sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The immediate reason is clear. The war involving the United States, Israel and Iran has disrupted energy supplies, particularly through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel prices in America have risen sharply, affecting farmers, truckers, businesses and ordinary households. With elections approaching, the administration is under pressure to bring down costs. There is nothing unusual about a government protecting its own economic interests. Every country is expected to do so. The problem arises when Washington expects other countries to follow one set of rules while keeping the freedom to change its own approach when circumstances demand it. If buying Russian fuel can be justified by American economic needs, India’s energy requirements deserve the same consideration. India cannot compromise its energy security India is one of the world’s largest energy consumers and depends heavily on imported crude oil. Its energy choices affect transport costs, inflation, agriculture, industry and the household budgets of millions of people. Russian crude oil became an important source for India and several allies after the Ukraine conflict because it was available at discounted prices. For India, buying Russian oil is not only a practical economic decision based on price, availability, and energy security, but also a decision made by a dependent ally, and in no way should it be seen as an endorsement of Moscow’s policies. India, time and again, has made it clear to the US and others that its energy decisions are guided by national interest. While the US can impose its own sanctions, it cannot dictate India’s energy choices. India should now be strong enough to stand firm against any attempt to turn oil purchases into a test of political loyalty. Trump’s latest move makes Washington’s earlier pressure on India more difficult to defend politically. If Russian oil revenues are the central concern, then American purchases of Russian diesel raise the same question: will the money earned by Moscow not also strengthen its economy? The argument is not that India and the United States face identical circumstances or that crude oil and refined diesel are exactly the same product. The legal arrangements may also differ. But the underlying principle remains: if a country’s own economic needs justify an exception, it should recognise that other countries have legitimate economic needs too. The arrangement also exposes the limits of sanctions as a foreign policy instrument. Sanctions can impose costs, but their effectiveness depends on consistency, international cooperation and credible enforcement. If restrictions are relaxed whenever the political price becomes too high, other countries may reasonably question whether the policy is based on principle or convenience. For India, this is an opportunity to make its case firmly without turning the issue into an unnecessary confrontation with Washington. India’s relationship with the United States is important across trade, technology, defence, education and the wider Indo-Pacific. New Delhi has no interest in allowing a disagreement over oil to damage cooperation in these areas and in no way, directly or indirectly, criticise it. However, a strong India-US partnership does not require India to accept every American demand. Strategic autonomy means maintaining the ability to make independent decisions while cooperating with other countries wherever interests converge. India should explain that its energy policy is neither directed against the United States nor intended to support any particular power. It is designed to ensure affordable and reliable supplies for a country of more than a billion people. New Delhi equally needs to remain conscious of the practical risks. We all understand that US sanctions and tariff measures can affect Indian exporters, banks, shipping companies and refiners. The answer is not to ignore these consequences, but to negotiate firmly, diversify energy sources and reduce excessive dependence on any single supplier. India should also continue investing in renewable energy, strategic petroleum reserves and long-term supply arrangements. These steps would provide greater protection against geopolitical shocks and reduce the ability of external powers to exert pressure through energy markets. The Russian diesel arrangement is unlikely, by itself, to resolve the global energy crisis. Supply disruptions linked to the West Asia, uncertainty around shipping routes and damage to energy infrastructure will continue to influence prices. But the episode offers India a clear diplomatic argument: what is good enough for America’s energy security cannot automatically be considered wrong for India’s. Washington has every right to pursue its national interests. India has the same right. The United States may use its laws to regulate transactions and impose sanctions, but it cannot reasonably expect India to treat American preferences as binding instructions in its foreign policy. IN the present century, data matters. New Delhi should make this point calmly, friendly, backed by facts and a clear assessment of its economic interests. It should avoid unnecessary rhetoric, but it should not surrender its decision-making space either. Finally, as is happening, New Delhi’s foreign policy must be guided by Indian interests. Partnerships with major powers are valuable, but they remain partnerships only when both sides recognise each other’s sovereignty. Trump’s Russian diesel deal has made that principle more relevant than ever.

stories.headline: US Democrats’ House victory could test Trump’s India policy
stories.title: US Democrats’ House victory could test Trump’s India policy
stories.summary: Washington, Oct 13 : Democrats are heavy favourites to win control of the US House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, according to the prediction markets and polling averages, raising the prospect of tougher congressional scrutiny of President Donald Trump's tariff, trade and visa policies that weigh heavily on India. Traders on the prediction market Kalshi gave Democrats a 90 per cent chance of taking the House and a 62 per cent chance of winning the Senate, according to prices published on Monday. Kalshi put the chance of a Democratic sweep of both chambers at 61 per cent. The next most likely outcome, at 30 per cent, was a divided Congress with Democrats running the House and Republicans keeping the Senate. The Silver Bulletin polling average, updated on Monday, had Democrats ahead by 8.8 points on the generic congressional ballot, which asks voters which party they will support for Congress. "Democrats' surge in the polls that started in early September still hasn't stopped," the Silver Bulletin said. Trump's own numbers offer his party little cover. A CBS News/YouGov poll conducted from September 30 to October 2 found 39 per cent of Americans approved of his job performance and 61 per cent disapproved. On inflation, only 29 per cent approved and 71 per cent disapproved. The Senate is far less certain. The Cook Political Report rates seven races as toss-ups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Six of those seats are held by Republicans. A Democratic House would give the party subpoena power and committee gavels. House Democrats are preparing "a vast oversight agenda" covering Trump, his family and his administration, US media said. London-based think tank Chatham House said Democrats' real leverage would be on money, even if they took only the House. The US debt limit is expected to be reached by mid-2027, and a Democratic House alone would rule out Republicans using the budget reconciliation process to raise it, Max Yoeli, a senior research fellow at Chatham House, wrote last month. Yoeli also cautioned that opposition on foreign policy "will be more about optics than hard constraints", since Democrats would lack the votes to override presidential vetoes. For India, that points to a Democratic House making its mark mostly through oversight rather than new law. Trump's tariffs have largely been imposed through executive action. A Democratic House could hold hearings and force votes on them, but would struggle to overturn them against a veto. The same applies to the Graham Act tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, which could take effect from October 18. The law requires the administration to send Congress a written justification at least 10 days before imposing such duties, a requirement that a Democratic-led House would be well placed to press. Any India-US trade agreement that needs legislation would also face a more sceptical chamber. The $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, which falls heavily on Indian professionals, is already tied up in court. A federal judge in California blocked its enforcement on September 30, and the administration has appealed to the Ninth Circuit. Democrats could add hearings and spending riders to that legal fight. Indian nationals have historically accounted for the largest share of H-1B beneficiaries. The four Indian-American members seeking re-election to the House, Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam, all Democrats, are in races rated safe for their party. The current House has six Indian-American members. Raja Krishnamoorthi gave up his seat to run for the Senate and lost the Illinois primary, while Shri Thanedar lost his Michigan primary in August. The House has 435 voting members, and a party needs 218 seats for a majority. All House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot on November 3. --IANS

stories.headline: SKUAST-K’s Green Campus Roadmap
stories.title: SKUAST-K’s Green Campus Roadmap
stories.summary: Climate change is no longer a far-off environmental concern confined to scientific discussions and policy documents. The Himalayan region of Kashmir stands at the centre of this emerging climate challenge. Extreme weather events have further intensified these problems. The devastating floods of 2014, which affected nearly 2.5 million people, claimed more than 280 lives, and caused estimated economic losses of around ₹1 lakh crore, remind us of Kashmir’s vulnerability to climate extremes. The unpredictability continues during 2026; J&K witnessed a marked increase in extreme rainfall events. According to the Director of the Meteorological Center, Kashmir, DrMukhtar Ahmad, 44 cloudbursts have struck Jammu and Kashmir since the onset of the monsoon this year, claiming about 35lives. These cloudburst incidents further triggered flash floods in Districts including Shopian, Anantnag, Bandipora and Budgam. The events have caused extensive damage to roads, bridges, homes and agricultural land, underscoring the region’s increasing vulnerability to climate-induced weather vagaries and the growing frequency of high-impact rainfall events. Universities as Climate Solution Hubs For a region where agriculture, horticulture, livestock, and natural resources sustain millions of livelihoods, climate resilience is now a necessity. In this backdrop, the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K) has developed and adopted its Green and Sustainable Campuses Policy, marking a paradigm shift from a conventional campus to a climate-smart institution. This Policy brings together the seven vast campuses, all research stations, and KrishiVigyanKendras (KVKs) to create a vibrant ecosystem that works towards resource-efficient, climate-smart, and low-carbon spaces, aligning itself with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Restoring Landscapes One of the major policy initiatives of SKUAST-K is its focus on restoring and reclaiming degraded landscapes and wastelands. The University has, on a massive scale, undertaken plantation, landscaping, and biodiversity enhancement initiatives across its campuses. Through cleaning drives, landscape development, and ecological rehabilitation, the neglected and degraded areas within university campuses have been systematically restored. The development of lawns, gardens, roadside landscapes, biodiversity spaces, and green recreational areas has transformed previously underutilized spaces into productive ecological assets. At its main campus in Shalimar, approximately 22,000 square feet of area has been converted into green lawn cover, along with the planting of 1,800 saplings of diverse species. These interventions have enhanced campus aesthetics and beautification besides aiding carbon sequestration, biodiversity enrichment, and improved microclimatic conditions. The university has extended its green restoration efforts past conventional landscaping. At the Faculty of Forestry in Benhama, Ganderbal, approximately 25,000 saplings have been planted on degraded southern hill slopes, including indigenous, arboreal, and selected exotic species, thereby supporting land restoration and biodiversity recovery. Similar plantation initiatives have also been undertaken at other campuses. Specialized biodiversity landscapes have also been developed, including Lavender and Rosemary Parks at the Faculty of Forestry, Benhama, which provide spaces for biodiversity conservation, experiential learning, and research. From Waste Management to Circular Agriculture A defining feature of SKUAST-K’s sustainability approach is its commitment to the circular economy—where waste is transformed into wealth. Across its campuses, research stations and extension centers, agricultural residues, crop waste, weeds and livestock manure are converted into compost and vermicompost, reducing dependence on chemical inputs while improving soil health. At the Shalimar campus, about 250 kg of kitchen waste is generated daily, which is then converted into nutrient-rich compost using mechanized composting units and used on university farms. Promoting the University’s vision of waste-to-wealth, the Mountain Livestock Research Institute produces approximately 200 tonnes of vermicompost annually, creating a sustainable model for a circular agricultural economy. The university is advancing conservation initiatives not only through landscape conservation reforms but also through a circular agri-economy. One of the university’s notable resource conservation initiatives involved refurbishing and repurposing old furniture rather than replacing it. The initiative resulted in savings of approximately ₹1.25 crore, reduced material waste, and freed over 4,000 square feet of storage space at the Shalimar campus—demonstrating that sustainability can also be economically efficient. Building Green Campuses Through Innovation To achieve its sustainability vision, the university is pursuing institutional transformation and has installed nearly 2,000 solar panels, 100 solar streetlights, and more than 15,000 LED bulbs across its campuses. Its paperless examination system alone saves approximately 22 lakh sheets of paper annually, equivalent to conserving around 264 trees, 44,000 liters of water, and notable energy resources. Digital governance initiatives, such as sustainability monitoring dashboards and paperless administrative processes, also demonstrate how technology can support environmental accountability. A Blueprint for Climate-Resilient Agriculture By embedding climate consciousness into governance, research, education, infrastructure, and extension, SKUAST-K is seriously pursuing the goal of sustaining tomorrow for future generations. Dr Nasir A Dar- Coordinator IQAC, SKUAST-K DrF.A.Lone- Head Environmental Science, SKUAST-K Dr Heeba Din, Editor,IQAC SKUAST-K

The University has, on a massive scale, undertaken plantation, landscaping, and biodiversity enhancement initiatives across its campuses.
Through cleaning drives, landscape development, and ecological rehabilitation, the neglected and degraded areas within university campuses have been systematically restored.
The development of lawns, gardens, roadside landscapes, biodiversity spaces, and green recreational areas has transformed previously underutilized spaces into productive ecological assets.

The university has extended its green restoration efforts past conventional landscaping.

stories.title: Delhi to host first-ever BIMSTEC Home Ministers’ meeting today
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 13 : India is set to host the first-ever BIMSTEC Home Ministers' Meeting in New Delhi on Tuesday, marking a significant step towards strengthening regional cooperation on security-related issues. Union Home Minister Amit Shah will chair the meeting. Describing the gathering as a historic occasion, HM Shah on Monday said the meeting underscores "our shared resolve to combat terrorism, transnational organised crime, narcotics radicalisation, trafficking, illicit financial flows, and cyber threats". "Through decisive coordination, we remain committed to building a safer, stronger, and more secure BIMSTEC," the Home Minister said. Officials from the member countries are expected to participate in the meeting. The meeting is expected to provide a platform for BIMSTEC member nations to discuss common security concerns and explore ways to enhance cooperation in addressing threats that extend across national borders. The gathering also highlights the importance of coordinated regional efforts to counter terrorism, organised criminal networks, drug-related threats, human trafficking and cybercrime. BIMSTEC, an acronym for the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation, is a regional organisation comprising seven member countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. According to the organisation's official website, BIMSTEC works to strengthen collaboration in areas such as agriculture and food security, the blue economy, connectivity, culture, disaster management, energy, environment and climate change, fiscal and monetary policy, health, human resource development, fisheries and livestock, and people-to-people relations, among other fields. In July this year, the 5th Meeting of the BIMSTEC National Security Chiefs was held in New Delhi, where the National Security Advisers and heads of delegations exchanged views on various measures to combat terrorism and organised crime; ensure security in the cyber, maritime and energy domains; enhance connectivity; facilitate efficient disaster management; and tackle new and emerging security threats. The meeting adopted the BIMSTEC Guidelines for the Maritime Component of Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief. The guidelines will help BIMSTEC member states undertake relief operations in the region in an expeditious manner. They also endorsed a set of Guiding Principles on the Conduct of Maritime Law Enforcement Agencies during Interactions at Sea. These principles are expected to provide reference points for increasing predictability and promoting safety during maritime engagements among member states. --IANS

stories.headline: Common Cause of “Vote Chori”: Opposition and Gen Z Protests Rattle Government as Supreme Court Steps In
stories.title: Common Cause of “Vote Chori”: Opposition and Gen Z Protests Rattle Government as Supreme Court Steps In
stories.summary: India’s democracy is facing a moment that demands constitutional introspection. The Opposition’s campaign against alleged “vote chori” has acquired wider significance as sections of Gen Z join the call for electoral accountability and the Supreme Court intervenes to protect peaceful protest and ordinary public movement. The convergence raises a question that cannot be answered merely through political rhetoric, police barricades or restrictions: can citizens trust the institutions responsible for safeguarding their democratic rights? Democracy derives legitimacy not simply from announced results, but from public confidence in the fairness of the process. “Vote Chori”: Allegations That Require Answers “Vote chori” expresses a basic concern: can every eligible Indian vote, and can the public trust the process? Controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has intensified these questions. Opposition parties have raised concerns about deletions, verification procedures and the Election Commission’s handling of objections. The Commission has defended revision as necessary to maintain accurate rolls, citing deaths, migration and duplicate entries. Allegations of deliberate manipulation must be tested through evidence, not treated as conclusively established. The issue cannot be dismissed because political parties have raised it. Electoral rolls are the foundation of representative democracy, and wrongful deletion can deprive an eligible voter of meaningful participation. The answer lies in transparent procedures, accessible corrections and independent scrutiny. Every disputed deletion should be explained and reviewed; credible evidence of irregularity should prompt investigation. The Election Commission’s independence is a public trust that must be sustained through transparent and fair conduct. Opposition and Gen Z: A Convergence Beyond Party Politics The protests reveal a new political convergence. The Opposition’s credibility depends on evidence, consistency and a willingness to pursue constitutional remedies. Young people’s participation adds another dimension. Gen Z has grown up with digital access and expects institutions to explain decisions, justify restrictions and respond to scrutiny. This convergence should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. Allegations require evidence, protests must remain peaceful, and public authorities retain the duty to maintain law and order. Criticism is not disloyalty, and dissent is not necessarily disorder. Electoral concerns call for engagement, verification and redress—not an assumption that questioners must be silenced. The Supreme Court’s Intervention The events surrounding protests in Delhi have raised a separate constitutional concern: how the State responds to peaceful dissent. On October 11, 2026, a special Supreme Court bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana addressed restrictions affecting protesters and public movement. The Court directed authorities to remove barricades that were not strictly warranted, ensure normal functioning of Metro and railway services, and prevent the unlawful detention of peaceful, unarmed protesters. These directions reaffirm familiar constitutional principles. The State may regulate assemblies and prevent violence, but restrictions must be lawful, pursue a legitimate objective and remain proportionate. A capital city cannot be turned into a zone of indiscriminate restriction merely because a demonstration is politically inconvenient. Disruptions to transport and limits on public assembly require justification grounded in law and necessity. Article 19 protects speech and peaceful assembly, subject to lawful restrictions; Articles 21 and 14 protect liberty and guard against arbitrary State action. These guarantees do not disappear when a government faces criticism. The Court’s intervention places the balance between public order and civil liberty under judicial scrutiny. Judicial Directions Are Not Optional The most serious concern arises from allegations that restrictions continued, or were implemented in ways inconsistent with the Court’s directions, despite judicial intervention. Claims of police excess and unlawful detention require fair examination; deliberate disobedience must be established judicially. The principle is clear: executive authorities cannot treat binding judicial directions as optional. If clarification is needed, they should seek it; they cannot substitute their preferences for a court’s order. Deliberate non-compliance, if established, would undermine judicial authority and public confidence; accountability must follow through lawful proceedings. Police must facilitate lawful activity, prevent violence and protect citizens. Force, detention and preventive restrictions must be justified by law and circumstances. Peaceful protesters cannot be treated as offenders merely because their message embarrasses those in power. Democracy Is More Than Winning Elections An elected government has a mandate to govern, not disregard constitutional limits. Equally, an Opposition cannot treat every defeat as proof of manipulation. The Election Commission should explain revision procedures, protect personal data while publishing relevant information, provide hearings to affected voters and address documented discrepancies. Political parties and civil society should present verifiable evidence. The judiciary must remain independent and impartial. The government must show its confidence in democracy by accepting scrutiny, while Parliament should consider strengthening safeguards for voter registration. The Constitutional Test The Opposition–Gen Z convergence is a reminder that public trust must be earned, not commanded. The government can answer allegations with facts and restore institutional confidence. It should not mistake the management of public order for the suppression of public opinion. A strong government is not one that prevents uncomfortable questions, but one that answers them convincingly. The Court has reiterated that constitutional government is defined by restraint as well as authority. Alleged irregularities and violations of judicial orders must be determined through evidence and due process. Neither slogans nor official denials can substitute for a credible examination of the facts. India’s democratic strength lies in its Constitution, independent institutions and citizens’ freedom to question those who govern them. “Vote chori” must ultimately be tested through evidence and accountability, but the slogan must not become an excuse to avoid scrutiny. The ballot belongs to the citizen; the Constitution binds the government; the judiciary safeguards the limits of State power; and peaceful dissent remains essential to democratic life. The real test of democracy is not whether those in power can silence their critics, but whether they can command public confidence while allowing their conduct to be questioned. That is the constitutional challenge before India today. (The Author is a Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India, Constitutional Thinker and a Public Intellectual)

article_sentences: Karnataka’s 56% reservation quota has been struck down by the High Court.
The state government plans to explore a Supreme Court appeal and has renewed its demand for a review of the 50% reservation ceiling.

Bengaluru: The Karnataka High Court has struck down the state’s decision to increase reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes beyond the 50% ceiling, ruling the enhanced quota unconstitutional.
The 2022 legislation increased reservation for Scheduled Castes from 15% to 17% and for Scheduled Tribes from 3% to 7%.
This took the overall reservation in Karnataka for education and government jobs to 56%.
Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara said the state government would pursue all available legal options, including filing an appeal before the Supreme Court.

In a statement issued on Monday evening, Parameshwara urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Union government to undertake a comprehensive review of the 50% reservation ceiling and consider constitutional and legislative measures to address Karnataka’s demand.
He also called on the Centre to reconsider the state’s request to include the enhanced reservation provisions in the Constitution’s Ninth Schedule.
Parameshwara said the BJP government, which enacted the legislation in October 2022, was aware that the changes would raise the overall reservation quota to 56%.
He argued that the legislation was passed without securing the requested Ninth Schedule protection, despite the issue having been recognised by the government at the time.

According to Parameshwara, the Centre informed Parliament on July 25, 2026, that Karnataka’s proposal for inclusion in the Ninth Schedule had been deferred because the matter was pending before the High Court.
Former chief minister Siddaramaiah also called on the Union government to explain how it intended to address the issue.

article_sentences: Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and 10 other INDIA bloc leaders on Monday, October 12, moved the Supreme Court challenging the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, seeking a suspension of the exercise across all states pending adjudication of their petition.

The petition seeks disclosure of the ECI's internal records relating to the SIR, judicial scrutiny of decisions taken by the poll panel, an independent audit of voter deletions and directions to ensure that no voter's name is removed without notice and an opportunity for a hearing.

The other petitioners include Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress leader Saugata Roy, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal leader Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut, CPI(M) leader MA Baby, CPI leader D Raja, Jharkhand Mukti Morcha leader Mahua Majhi, NCP (Sharad Pawar) leader Supriya Sule and Indian Union Muslim League leader ET Mohammed Basheer.
The petition names the ECI, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as respondents.
It was filed through advocate-on-record S Prasanna.
The petition alleges that the CEC exercised the Election Commission's collective powers without the knowledge, approval or concurrence of the other Election Commissioners.

It relies on an Indian Express investigation published on September 23, which reported that Sandhu and Joshi had recorded objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months to decisions taken under Kumar.
The petition states that the ECI's position is that its decisions were unanimous, while media reports based on records suggest otherwise.
"The question can be answered only by examining the Commission's records," the plea states.
The petition argues that the issue goes beyond internal administrative procedure.
"The issue is not merely one of internal administrative procedure," it states.

stories.headline: Dignity of asking questions restored
stories.title: Dignity of asking questions restored
stories.summary: Frankly speaking, I am not going to assess the performance of the Omar Abdullah government over the past two years. It is quite unfair to judge a government that is not even half as empowered as the governments I have seen since late 1970s. A government in Jammu and Kashmir was never a complete one, because it was always sought to be guided by forces other than those elected to govern. This has been true since the times of Sheikh Abdullah, even when he was regarded as the supreme leader and the state enjoyed the full autonomy that his descendants are yearning for today. Had the governments in J&K been given the authority to govern, Sheikh Abdullah would not have been deposed in 1953. Historians have the right to ask: if his government was dismissed for harbouring secessionist thoughts, why was he brought back to power? Congress owes this answer to the nation. Fast forward this to 2026: as Omar Abdullah the first Chief Minister of the Union Territory is about to complete two years in office in a couple of days, the complexities have multiplied. Today is the time to analyze things since October 8, 2024—the day the results of the Assembly polls made it clear that the National Conference, along with its allies, had won a majority of seats. Yet, it took eight days for his swearing-in ceremony. This is a rare period in the history of Jammu and Kashmir—not just because there are two overlapping centers of authority ordained by the UT status, but because of the kind of political, social, and cultural narratives it has engendered. It felt like a civilizational rebirth in Kashmir when people saw a reflection of their urges and aspirations in the government they voted to power. Notwithstanding the election results and the hyperbolic greetings offered to democracy in Jammu and Kashmir, the elected National Conference-Congress government has had to contend with an entrenched perception that the Abdullahs’ party represents a Kashmir-oriented political project. A lot of commentary, containing some very fair points, has been written and spoken by the opposition parties—the BJP in particular, though local opposition groups have been equally critical and harsh—in assessing the government’s performance and declaring it unsuccessful in delivering on its manifesto promises. The opposition has an inherent right in a democratic setup to assess and reassess the performance of the government, but the repeated questioning of the mandate itself goes against the established norms of a functioning democracy. The opposition could not have ignored the issues that concern the people. They challenged the government on everything from electricity supply to the regularization of daily wagers and jobs for the jobless. They pointed out the wide gaps between the manifesto promises and the actual reality on the ground. All the opposition groups, both within the legislature and outside of it, were on the same page regarding one thing: that the issue of statehood was a major distraction from day-to-day governance. And it is true that a common person worries more about daily issues than wider political ones—until they realize those broader issues are impinging on their land, individual and family dignity, and on a larger scale, the community and the whole territory. National Conference could not take its narrative to the grassroots level that the statehood was quite essential. Its leadership did speak of it but it could not convince the masses that it was not the party project but something what was historic and question of the day-to-day dignity of the people. There is no doubt that the local unit took upon itself to derail this project. The opposition deliberately ignored the actual reality and the way system operated without powers. This was way to distract attention from their own era of controlling the system. Daily governance issues are intrinsically linked to daily dignity. This dignity is common to all communities—Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, and Buddhists. It is the responsibility of the state to uphold this. There can be no separate dignity for different communities. To date, despite all his logical and persuasive arguments, Omar has not been able to secure statehood—his central mantra for improving governance within the system and on the ground. This is not entirely in his hands. The Centre has to go back to the drawing board and consider whether it is standing in the way of Omar Abdullah’s pursuit for the restoration of statehood, or if it has discovered new hurdles preventing the return of the status it had promised. There should be some clarity on this; if there is going to be further delay, it should be specified. That is what Omar is demanding to know. Since there are no specific answers, it raises a bigger question: is the elected government still being viewed through prism of old prejudices? In the context of Jammu and Kashmir, the question is not just political or administrative, but geopolitical and geostrategic. That requires a wider understanding of the situation and its requirements. In the current arrangement, accountability has become a one-way street. The elected government is held accountable for whatever goes wrong because it is the one meant to be questioned by the people. But things turn bizarre when voices start emerging from within the system itself, questioning the elected government over incidents that fall completely outside its jurisdiction. This undermines the real-time concept of accountability and stretches the elected government’s responsibility too far. Omar, as a politician, is not pleased with such criticism. He has built his own line of defense. At times, he brushes aside tough questions. Yet, what cannot be ignored is that he faces questions—and more often than not, he answers them. This dynamic has returned to Kashmir after a gap of many years. Today, questions are not formulated or prefaced with the vocabulary of flattery; they are tough. His answers provide a definitive perspective on critically important issues for the nation on the international stage, as well as for Jammu and Kashmir. His willingness to encourage questions and face open-media-byte sessions on a daily basis has conferred a dignity to both the aspirations and the skepticism of ordinary people.

article_sentences: The South Peninsula is bracing for the arrival of the north-east monsoon, with the seasonal reversal of winds expected to gather momentum alongside the retreat of the south-west monsoon.

The trigger could be a low-pressure area forecast to develop over the south-east Bay of Bengal anytime now, setting the stage for the easterly flows that herald the onset of the second rainy season for the water-starved region.
The atmospheric signals are falling into place, with an upper-air cyclonic circulation over the South Andaman Sea poised to descend to lower levels and consolidate into the crucial low-pressure area.
At the western end of the Bay, another cyclonic circulation over the Gulf of Mannar could help draw in and channel the easterly winds, carrying the north-east monsoon deeper into the South Peninsula.
With the Bay of Bengal primed for a fresh low-pressure system and the retreating monsoon nearing its final exit, the South Peninsula is entering a consequential phase of the seasonal calendar.

The coming days will determine how quickly the easterlies take charge, and whether the expected onset of north-east monsoon brings a sustained spell of rain to the region after the south-west monsoon’s long retreat.
The emerging weather pattern is already offering a foretaste of the transition, with rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds unfolding over several parts of southern India.
These conditions could intensify on either side of October 15, around which the north-east monsoon is likely to set in over Tamil Nadu and adjoining areas.
Its formal arrival could be announced during this phase.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), in its Tuesday morning assessment, said conditions were becoming favourable for the south-west monsoon to withdraw from the remaining parts of the country and for north-east monsoon rains to commence over the South Peninsula simultaneously during the next 2-3 days.
The withdrawal line of the four-month south-west monsoon, which officially ended on September 30, continues to pass through Kolkata, Angul, Khammam and Honavar.
The predecessor monsoon must complete its retreat from the mainland before the seasonal transition is fully established, although the two processes can overlap in time.
